title: What is exploding head syndrome?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss exploding head syndrome, a benign parasomnia in which people hear a loud booming noise (gunshot, cymbal crash, explosion) as they fall asleep or wake, often with a pounding heart and occasionally an electrical sensation. They cover Chuck's Facebook survey of respondents, the 1870s description by Silas Weir Mitchell (patient "Mr V"), the naming by neurologist John MS Pierce in The Lancet, prevalence figures (about 10 percent of people, higher in psychiatric patients and women in their fifties), the leading theory of a brainstem reticular formation glitch with alpha wave suppression and a burst of activity in hearing regions, other theories (middle ear, seizures, drug withdrawal, calcium ion channels), management through diagnosis and sleep hygiene, and differences from PTSD. The episode closes with a listener mail from Kate about visiting Chernobyl.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about sleep, cutting back on drinking, and tonic water, then introduce exploding head syndrome as a nighttime hallucination and parasomnia.

segments.title: Introduction and naming of exploding head syndrome
segments.summary: Josh describes the syndrome as a loud sound heard while falling asleep, compares it to sleep paralysis, and discusses the name. Chuck reports a Facebook survey that drew about 150 responses, mostly from women, with varied anecdotes.

segments.title: Symptoms and who gets it
segments.summary: The hosts describe the loud noise, the startle and racing heart, lack of pain, and that onset tends to be in the fifties with women at higher risk. They note a reported case in a ten year old.

segments.title: History: Silas Weir Mitchell and naming by John MS Pierce
segments.summary: Silas Weir Mitchell described the sensation in the 1870s, including patient Mr V, and called them sensory discharges. Neurologist John MS Pierce in The Lancet later gave the condition its name.

segments.title: Prevalence and associations
segments.summary: About 18 percent of college students in one study reported it, though experts think that is high, and about 10 percent is the commonly settled estimate. It is more common in psychiatric patients and less common in people with other sleep disorders.

segments.title: Causes: brainstem glitch and other theories
segments.summary: The hosts explain falling asleep as the brain shutting down regions. The leading theory is a glitch in the brainstem reticular formation that suppresses alpha waves and triggers a burst of activity in hearing regions. Other theories include middle ear dysfunction, epilepsy (ruled out by EEG in some cases), benzodiazepine withdrawal, and calcium ion channels.

segments.title: Management, sleep hygiene, and PTSD distinction
segments.summary: Diagnosis alone often ends episodes and stress may play a role. Patients may be mistaken for stroke or epilepsy. The condition differs from PTSD flashbacks. Sleep hygiene advice such as regular schedule, quiet and dark room, avoiding screens, and no booze or coffee after five is discussed.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off plug
segments.summary: Hosts suggest searching for the topic on HowStuffWorks and mention the Facebook study.

segments.title: Listener mail: Chernobyl visit
segments.summary: Kate from Nottingham describes visiting the Chernobyl exclusion zone and the abandoned town of Pripyat, and notes the Soviet government delayed evacuation and that workers saved reactor three.
